title: TickLens
user: Indie browser-game developers trying to find why room updates lag long before CPU appears saturated.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A Node/Socket.IO game developer sees lag at 500 players despite low CPU; replies point to I/O throughput and accidentally quadratic outbound updates.
A multiplayer user needs separate server/client paths and encounters authority errors, showing that state topology becomes hard to see as games grow.

recurrence: A current production-scale report and ongoing engine-level multiplayer complexity point to a visibility gap rather than a mere framework choice.
current_workaround: Add ad-hoc logs, inspect CPU dashboards, or guess at Socket.IO traffic patterns.
incumbents_and_gap: Datadog and OpenTelemetry are infrastructure-first; game engines expose state but do not make per-room fanout and tick cost legible.
smallest_useful_product: Drop-in JS client/server probe that records tick duration, room size, bytes/messages per room, and emits a self-contained HTML trace. Non-goals: hosting, matchmaking, packet capture, engine lock-in.
success_measure: In a seeded 500-client test, users identify the highest fanout room from the report in under five minutes.
monetization: freemium — open local reports build trust; paid team retention/compare reports can fund it.
constraints: No payload capture by default; redact IDs; overhead budget under 2%; Socket.IO/WebSocket adapters initially only.
why_distinct: It diagnoses game-state fanout, not generic server performance.
